summary: This RFC extends CalDAV calendar access with a standard way to do scheduling operations on iCalendar-based events and tasks, such as invitations and replies. It defines the calendar-auto-schedule feature.

plainLanguage.summary: When you add an event to a shared calendar, other people should be told about it and be able to accept or decline. This document defines how a CalDAV server does that on its own, without each client inventing its own method.

questions: what is a caldav scheduling inbox
how does caldav request free busy time
subtitle: Lets a calendar server send invitations and collect replies for the events its users create.

tldr.problem: CalDAV servers can store calendars, but without a standard way to schedule, every client had to invent its own way of sending invitations, replies and cancellations.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds scheduling to CalDAV: a server watches for calendar data that names attendees, sends the matching iTIP messages itself, records what happened in new iCalendar parameters and HTTP headers, and answers busy time requests.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from June 2012, updated by RFC 7953, and it is the scheduling feature that CalDAV servers are expected to support.

today: RFC 6638 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2012. It is updated by RFC 7953 and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the definition of CalDAV scheduling.

sections.title: What CalDAV Scheduling Adds
sections.content:
The document specifies extensions to the CalDAV "calendar-access" feature (RFC 4791) that enable scheduling of iCalendar-based calendar components between calendar users. It leans on the scheduling methods defined in the iCalendar Transport-independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP, RFC 5546) so that users can schedule, reschedule, respond to a request, cancel a component, and search for busy time information. Some iTIP features are not covered: publishing, countering, delegating, refreshing and forwarding calendar components, and replacing the organizer of a component. Future extensions are expected to address those.

The model is client and server. The server is responsible for sending scheduling messages and processing incoming ones. The client only has to create, modify or delete a calendar component, and the server then delivers whatever messages are needed to the other calendar users. This is sometimes called implicit scheduling.

Only scheduling between users on a single system is addressed, so scheduling between two different CalDAV servers is not defined. The specification is, however, compatible with servers that send or receive scheduling messages with external users, for example using the iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol (iMIP, RFC 6047).

Three parts of the document carry the weight: Section 3 defines the automated scheduling operations that let a client store iCalendar data and have the server act on it, Section 4 defines how the server processes the resulting scheduling messages, and Section 5 defines how freebusy requests get an immediate response. Section 6 defines the access control privileges for these operations. The discussion is mostly about scheduling events, but scheduling of to-dos is supported in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: The client saves the event and forgets about invitations. The server notices that the event names other people and sends the invitations itself.

sections.title: The Inbox, the Outbox and the User's Addresses
sections.content:
A server supporting these features is REQUIRED to support the CalDAV calendar-access feature, and includes "calendar-auto-schedule" as a field in the DAV response header of an OPTIONS request on any resource that supports scheduling operations, properties, privileges or methods. The specification introduces new collection resource types and new scheduling privileges. It is the server's job to create these collections; clients have no way to create or delete them.

The scheduling Outbox collection is where busy time requests are aimed and where the privileges for outgoing scheduling requests are managed. It MUST report the DAV:collection and CALDAV:schedule-outbox elements in its resource type, and it MUST NOT be a child at any depth of a calendar collection. The scheduling Inbox collection holds copies of incoming scheduling messages, either requests from an organizer or replies from an attendee, and it too is where the privileges for those are managed. It MUST report the DAV:collection and CALDAV:schedule-inbox elements, MUST NOT contain any collection resources, and MUST NOT be a child of a calendar collection.

Two properties on principal resources point to these collections. CALDAV:schedule-outbox-URL gives the URL of the scheduling Outbox owned by that principal; if it is absent, the calendar user is not enabled for sending scheduling messages. CALDAV:schedule-inbox-URL does the same for the Inbox and for receiving messages. A third property, CALDAV:calendar-user-address-set, lists the calendar addresses of the principal and is needed to map the addresses used in iCalendar data to principals and their collections; support for it is REQUIRED, and if it is absent the calendar user is not enabled for scheduling at all. A fourth, CALDAV:calendar-user-type, carries the same values as the iCalendar CUTYPE parameter, so a client searching for attendees can restrict the search to people or to rooms.
sections.plainLanguage: Each user has two special folders on the server: an outbox where outgoing requests are aimed, and an inbox where incoming requests arrive. The server also records the email addresses that count as belonging to each user.

sections.title: Organizer Events and Attendee Events
sections.content:
When a calendar object resource is created, modified or removed, the server examines the calendar data to see whether it represents a scheduling object resource. If it does, the server automatically attempts to deliver a scheduling message to the appropriate calendar users. The operations are equivalent to the iTIP REQUEST, REPLY, CANCEL and ADD methods.

A calendar object resource is a valid organizer scheduling object resource when the ORGANIZER property is present and set in all of its calendar components to a value that matches one of the calendar user addresses of the owner of the calendar collection. It is a valid attendee scheduling object resource when the ORGANIZER property is present and set in all components to the same value, that value does not match an address of the owner, and at least one ATTENDEE property value matches an address of the owner. Attendee scheduling object resources are usually created by the server, in a suitable calendar collection.

The server's behaviour then depends on who owns the resource. An organizer may create, modify or remove a resource, subject to access privileges, preconditions and the restrictions CalDAV places on calendar objects. When the organizer is also an attendee of the same component, the server MUST NOT send a scheduling message to that attendee. The server SHOULD reject any attempt to set the participation status of another user's ATTENDEE property to a value other than NEEDS-ACTION unless the SCHEDULE-AGENT parameter is present and set to SERVER.
sections.plainLanguage: Whether the server sends invitations depends on who owns the event and who is named in it. An event you own triggers invitations; an event you were invited to triggers a reply.

sections.title: What the Server Does When an Event Changes
sections.content:
On create, the server inspects each ATTENDEE property to decide whether to send a scheduling message, taking the SCHEDULE-AGENT parameter into account. With the default value SERVER the server sends an iTIP REQUEST; with CLIENT or NONE it sends nothing. The server MUST add a SCHEDULE-STATUS parameter to each ATTENDEE property it creates a message for and set its value as described below. That means the stored resource differs from what the client sent, so clients MAY reload the calendar data to pick up the server-generated state. The server MUST NOT set SCHEDULE-STATUS on an attendee for which it did not attempt delivery. If the organizer attempts a forbidden change, the server MUST return an error with the CALDAV:allowed-organizer-scheduling-object-change precondition code.

On modify, the server compares the original and the modified iCalendar data per instance to decide what to send. If an attendee is removed, the server sends CANCEL. If an attendee is added, it sends REQUEST or ADD. If an attendee stays and the event changed, it sends REQUEST. The comparison is per attendee and per SCHEDULE-AGENT value, and the server again updates the SCHEDULE-STATUS parameters. On remove, the server inspects each ATTENDEE property and sends the matching message, normally CANCEL.

When the server receives a scheduling message it processes it according to whether it came from an organizer or an attendee: requests, additions and cancellations lead to the event being placed in the recipient's default calendar collection, and replies update the participation status recorded in the organizer's copy. A default calendar is needed when a recipient has none, and the CALDAV:default-calendar-needed and CALDAV:valid-schedule-default-calendar-URL preconditions report that case.

Busy time is handled separately. The requester sends a POST to its own scheduling Outbox collection with a VFREEBUSY calendar component whose METHOD property is set to REQUEST, and the ORGANIZER value must match one of the calendar user's addresses. The response is an XML document with a CALDAV:schedule-response root element holding one CALDAV:response element per calendar user, each naming the user, giving a scheduling status and error codes, and, for a successful request, the busy time information itself as a VFREEBUSY component.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding someone to an event sends them an invitation. Changing the event sends an update. Removing them or the event sends a cancellation. Separately, you can ask the server when people are busy.

sections.title: Delivery and Reply Status Codes
sections.content:
Two kinds of status come back when scheduling with an attendee. The first is a delivery status, which says whether the message from the organizer to the attendee was delivered. The second is a reply status, which corresponds to the attendee's own REQUEST-STATUS information in the reply sent back to the organizer. When an attendee replies to the organizer there is delivery status for that message, but no REQUEST-STATUS comes back, so there is no equivalent reply status.

The delivery status travels in the SCHEDULE-STATUS parameter. Code 1.0 means the message is pending, because the server is still trying to send it, and the value is expected to change once sending and delivery have been attempted. Code 1.1 means the message was sent successfully but the server has no explicit information about whether it was delivered, which can happen with store-and-forward protocols such as iMIP. Code 1.2 means the message was delivered. Code 3.7 means it was not delivered because the server did not recognise the calendar user address as a valid calendar user. Code 3.8 means it was not delivered because of insufficient privileges. Code 5.1 means the server could not complete delivery, likely a temporary failure, so the originator may try again later. Code 5.2 means the server found no way to deliver it, likely a permanent failure, so the originator ought to check or correct the address. Code 5.3 means delivery was rejected because scheduling with that recipient is not allowed.

The reply status can be any of the valid iTIP REQUEST-STATUS values. The 1.xx codes are new, and this specification restricts them: for a 1.xx code, all components MUST have exactly the same code. Status 1.0 is Pending, 1.1 is Sent and 1.2 is Delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: The server records what happened to each invitation: still trying, sent but delivery unknown, delivered, or failed with a reason. The codes say whether trying again would be worth it.

sections.title: The iCalendar Parameters That Drive Scheduling
sections.content:
Three iCalendar property parameters are added. SCHEDULE-AGENT says who is expected to deliver scheduling messages to that organizer or attendee. Its value is SERVER, CLIENT, NONE, or an experimental or registered token, and when the parameter is absent the value SERVER MUST be used. With SERVER the server sends the message, with CLIENT the client handles it, and with NONE no message is sent at all. Servers and clients MUST NOT include the parameter in scheduling messages they send, and unrecognised x-name and iana-token values must be treated as if they were NONE.

SCHEDULE-FORCE-SEND forces a message to be sent where the server would otherwise send none, for example when the event did not change in a way that warrants a new message. An organizer may set it to REQUEST on an attendee, and an attendee may set it to REPLY on the organizer. Its value must be a registered iCalendar METHOD value. Servers MUST NOT preserve it in the stored resource nor include it in scheduling messages, and clients MUST NOT include it in messages they send themselves. A server that sees an unrecognised value sets SCHEDULE-STATUS to 2.3, meaning success with an invalid property parameter ignored.

SCHEDULE-STATUS carries the status codes returned from processing the most recent scheduling message sent to that attendee or received from that organizer. Servers MUST only add or change it on attendee properties for users who were actually sent a message, and MUST add it to organizer properties for users who actually sent a reply. Clients SHOULD NOT change or remove a value the server supplied, unless the client is handling scheduling itself, in which case it may set the value to record the last message it received.
sections.plainLanguage: Three extra labels on the event data control the flow. One says who sends the invitation, one says send it even though nothing changed, and one records what happened when it was sent.

sections.title: New HTTP Headers and Avoiding Conflicts
sections.content:
Three HTTP headers are added. Schedule-Reply is a request header with the value "T" or "F". When an attendee removes a scheduling object resource and the header is "T" or absent, the server MUST send a reply message with the attendee's participation status set to DECLINED. When it is "F", the server MUST NOT send a scheduling message. That lets a client silently remove an unwanted scheduling message, for security or privacy reasons. The Schedule-Tag response header carries the current value of the CALDAV:schedule-tag property, and all scheduling object resources MUST support it. The If-Schedule-Tag-Match request header makes a method conditional on that value, so a client can avoid overwriting changes; all scheduling object resources MUST support it too.

These headers exist because scheduling object resources change often: attendees change their participation status, which updates the organizer's copy and refreshes the other attendees' copies. That produces changes which do not affect the client's own participation status, and the client would otherwise have to reload the data and reconcile it. Instead the server can merge a client's changes with the ones it made itself. When the If-Schedule-Tag-Match header is present, servers MUST automatically resolve conflicts caused by inconsequential changes; the header applies only to the request URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Because other people's replies keep changing your copy of an event, the server hands out a version number for it. Send that number back and the server merges your change with the one it made, instead of making you sort it out.

sections.title: Security, Privacy and iTIP Threats
sections.content:
Scheduling means sending and receiving messages, so the usual messaging security problems apply, in particular verifying the authenticity of the scheduling messages. Servers and clients MUST use an HTTP connection protected with TLS for all scheduling operations. Clients MUST verify the authenticity of the server, and servers MUST use HTTP authentication to verify the authenticity of the calendar user the client is acting for.

Servers MUST ensure that clients cannot consume excessive server resources with large scheduling operations, and SHOULD enforce the maximum resource size, maximum instances and maximum attendees per instance preconditions on the Inbox and Outbox collections.

When handling a scheduling operation, servers MUST check five things: that the owner of the calendar collection has a scheduling Outbox; that the authenticated user holds the schedule-send privilege on that Outbox; that messages are only delivered where the recipient's Inbox grants the schedule-deliver privilege; that the ORGANIZER property matches one of the owner's calendar user addresses, to prevent impersonation; and that the UID of a new resource does not match an existing resource with a different ORGANIZER, to prevent spoofing. Busy time requests are checked in a similar way.

On privacy, the specification only defines scheduling between users on the same server, and unauthenticated users have no way to carry out scheduling operations at all. Access control privileges decide which users may schedule with which others, and a user who does not want to expose calendar information can deny privileges, for all scheduling operations or for freebusy alone. The Schedule-Reply header with the value "F" lets an attendee delete a scheduling message without telling the organizer. Servers MUST NOT expose private iCalendar data or WebDAV resource state information about one calendar user to another through scheduling messages or error responses, and authorization errors MUST take preference over other errors. Of the iTIP threats, spoofing the organizer, spoofing the attendee, unauthorized replacement of the organizer, eavesdropping, data integrity and flooding are all addressed; unauthorized REFRESH requests are not, because this specification does not support the REFRESH method.
sections.plainLanguage: Invitations travel over an encrypted connection, the server checks who is allowed to send and receive them, and nobody's private calendar details leak into an error message or a reply.

items.label: PENDING
items.desc: The server is still trying to send the message.

items.label: SENT
items.desc: Sent, but delivery to the recipient is unknown.

items.label: DELIVERED
items.desc: The message was sent and delivered.

items.label: UNKNOWN USER
items.desc: The calendar user address was not recognised as valid.

items.label: NO PRIVILEGE
items.desc: Delivery failed because of insufficient privileges.

items.label: TEMPORARY FAILURE
items.desc: Delivery could not be completed; trying again later may work.

items.label: PERMANENT FAILURE
items.desc: No way to deliver it; check the recipient's address.

items.label: NOT ALLOWED
items.desc: Delivery was rejected because scheduling with that recipient is not allowed.
